t: Count Elements With Strictly Smaller and Greater Elements — Drop the Extremes
o: An element qualifies unless it equals the global minimum or the global maximum: any strictly-in-between value automatically has both a strictly smaller and a strictly greater element present somewhere in the array. In [11,7,2,15] only 2 (the min) and 15 (the max) fail the test, leaving 2 elements. Duplicates of interior values all count — [-3,3,3,90] yields 2 because both 3s have −3 below and 90 above. The subtle case is an all-equal array: there min = max and the naive formula n − count(min) − count(max) would go negative, while the true answer is simply 0. With n ≤ 100 any polynomial method passes, but the counting identity achieves a couple of linear passes and O(1) space.
k: Qualifying elements are exactly those strictly between min(nums) and max(nums).
Answer = n − count(min) − count(max), guarded to 0 when min == max.
Strictness applies to values, not positions: duplicates of interior values all count.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort and Trim Boundary Runs
a.i: After sorting, the answer is the number of elements between the run of minimums at the front and the run of maximums at the back. Two pointers peel duplicates off both ends; if they cross, every element was equal and the answer is 0.
s: Advance i past all copies of nums[0]; retreat j past all copies of nums[n − 1].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the two trimming scans are linear.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary — in-place sort (ignoring the sort's internal buffer).

a.i: Locate lo and hi and count their frequencies; every element equal to neither survives. The identity n − cnt(lo) − cnt(hi) is exact unless lo == hi (all values equal), where the correct answer is 0 instead of the formula's negative value.
s: Scan once for the minimum lo and the maximum hi.
Otherwise return n minus the frequency of lo minus the frequency of hi.
a.t: O(n) — three linear sweeps (min, max, count).

w: State the strictness observation out loud — it collapses the whole problem to excluding the extremes. The intended trap is the all-equal array, where the formula returns a negative number; guard it explicitly (or clamp with max(0, …)). Note that Math.min(...nums)-style spreads are fine at n ≤ 100 but would risk stack limits on huge inputs. Follow-up variants: count elements with at least k distinct smaller values, or solve it without modifying the input when memory is constrained.
